lessons.title: Choose the right AI coding tool for the task in front of you
lessons.summary: Compare Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor on how they work, where they live, and what each is best at, and build a quick habit for picking the right one per task instead of defaulting to whichever you opened first.
lessons.goal: Match a coding task to the AI tool best suited for it, using a short checklist instead of habit or hype.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most developers in 2026 have access to more than one coding agent - Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor all do agentic, multi-file coding now, and none of them is universally best. Picking the wrong one for a task wastes usage allowance or produces worse results than another tool would have on the same task. Knowing each tool's shape (CLI vs IDE vs cloud-task runner), sign-in model, and standout feature lets you switch deliberately instead of getting stuck in one tool by inertia.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Accounts or trial access to at least two of: Claude Code (via a Claude Pro/Max plan), Codex (via a ChatGPT Plus/Pro plan), and Cursor. You don't need all three to do this lesson, but the exercise works best with at least two.
steps: Learn the shape of each tool: Claude Code is a CLI/desktop/web/IDE-extension agent built around CLAUDE.md and Plan Mode; Codex is a ChatGPT-account agent with CLI, IDE extension, and cloud tasks that return PRs; Cursor is a full AI-first IDE (a VS Code fork) built around Tab autocomplete and Agent mode.

Note what each is billed against: Claude Code draws from your Claude Pro/Max session limits; Codex draws from your ChatGPT plan's rolling 5-hour window (or an API key); Cursor uses its own subscription and usage-credit pool.

Match task shape to tool: deep multi-step reasoning across an unfamiliar codebase favors Claude Code or Cursor Agent mode; a well-scoped bug fix or feature you want delegated end-to-end as a PR favors Codex's cloud tasks; fast in-editor iteration with autocomplete favors Cursor.
Check where the task already lives: an assigned GitHub issue fits Codex cloud tasks well; a task you're actively pairing on fits Claude Code or Cursor in an interactive session.
Run the tool-fit checklist below on a real task you have right now.
Try the same small task in two different tools if you have access, and compare the output quality, not just the speed.
Write down which tool you chose and why - this becomes a habit faster if you make the reasoning explicit the first few times.
lessons.prompt:
Task: [DESCRIBE THE TASK IN 1-2 SENTENCES]
Repo context: solo project or team-owned repo? [ANSWER]
Where do you already work day to day: terminal, VS Code, or JetBrains? [ANSWER]
Shape of the work: quick single-file edit, multi-file feature needing a plan, a bug that needs root-cause investigation, or a task you want to hand off entirely and review as a PR? [ANSWER]
What are you already paying for: Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT Plus/Pro, Cursor? [ANSWER]

Given these answers, which of Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor fits this task best, and why? If two are close, say what would break the tie.
lessons.explanation: The checklist forces the same four questions every time: tool shape, billing, task shape, and existing spend - the factors that actually predict a good fit, rather than 'which one do I like.' Asking 'what would break the tie' matters because many real tasks fit two tools reasonably well, and the honest answer is often 'either works, pick the one you already have open.' Running the checklist on a real task, not a hypothetical, is what makes the habit stick.
lessons.example: A developer needs to fix a flaky integration test that spans several files. The task needs root-cause investigation, not a quick edit, which rules out pure autocomplete-driven work. They run the investigation in Claude Code (deep multi-file reasoning, Plan Mode), then hand the confirmed fix to a Codex cloud task to open as a reviewable PR while they move on to other work - using two tools deliberately instead of one by default.
lessons.exercise: Pick one real task from your current backlog. Fill out the tool-fit checklist above with honest answers. Then open whichever tool you selected in your own account and give it the task, keeping the scope small enough to review in one sitting.
lessons.expectedResult: You can state in one sentence why you picked the tool you picked, and the tool's output matches the kind of task you gave it - e.g. a delegated bug fix on Codex returns a reviewable PR, or a repo-exploration task on Claude Code returns a cited explanation, not a half-finished edit.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to whatever tool is already open instead of checking whether the task shape actually fits it.
Ignoring billing overlap - running heavy exploration in one tool and heavy implementation in another without noticing both are consuming separate paid allowances for one task.
Assuming the tool you're fastest with today is automatically the right one for a task shape you haven't tried it on yet.
lessons.proTip: These tools are increasingly combinable, not exclusive: use Cursor or Claude Code for daily interactive work, and reserve Codex cloud tasks for well-specced work you can hand off and review later as a batch of PRs. The skill worth building is routing tasks, not picking a permanent favorite.

lessons.title: Understand an unfamiliar repository with an AI agent before you touch it
lessons.summary: Use Claude Code or Cursor in read-only exploration to build a cited, verifiable map of a codebase's structure, one real request flow, and its test setup before making any changes.
lessons.goal: Produce an accurate, citation-backed overview of an unfamiliar repository's architecture and one real code path through it.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every developer eventually inherits code someone else wrote - a new job, a client handoff, an open-source dependency you need to patch. Coding agents can read an entire repository in minutes, but only if you ask for citations and force an explicit 'trace one real flow' instead of accepting a plausible-sounding generic summary. Doing this in a read-only pass first, before any edit, is what prevents changes based on a wrong mental model of how the code actually works.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real repository you have access to - a work project or a cloned open-source repo. Claude Code or Cursor installed and signed in.
steps: Open the repo and start the agent in a read-only or exploration-only mode - in Claude Code, stay in Plan Mode (Shift+Tab) or explicitly say 'do not edit anything'; in Cursor, use Chat rather than Agent mode for this pass.
Ask for a guided tour: what the project does, its entry point(s), and its top-level directory layout.
Ask it to trace one specific, real flow through the code file by file, citing paths - e.g. what happens when a user submits a form, or how an incoming request is routed and handled.
Ask how the test suite is structured and the exact command that runs it.
Check whether the repo already has a CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, or .cursor/rules/ directory.
If none exists, ask the agent to draft one from what it actually found in the repo, for your review - do not accept it unread or unverified.
Open at least two of the file paths the agent cited yourself and confirm they say what it claimed.
Save the summary somewhere your team can find it - README, wiki, or onboarding doc.
lessons.prompt:
You are in read-only/exploration mode. Do not edit any files. Give me:
1. A one-paragraph summary of what this project does.
2. The main entry point file(s), with exact paths.
3. The top-level directory structure and what each major folder is for.
4. A step-by-step trace of what happens when [DESCRIBE ONE REAL FLOW, e.g. 'a user submits the checkout form'], citing the specific files and functions involved, in order.
5. The exact command(s) to run the test suite.
For anything you are not confident about, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
lessons.explanation: Requiring citations - specific file paths, in the order they're actually touched - forces the agent to ground its answer in what it read rather than produce a generic, plausible-sounding architecture description. Tracing one concrete flow end to end is more useful than an abstract summary because it's directly checkable: you can open the cited files yourself. The explicit 'say so if you're not confident' instruction reduces the chance of a confident wrong answer on the parts of the codebase the agent is less sure about.
lessons.example: A developer joins a project and points Claude Code at an unfamiliar Next.js e-commerce repo, asking it to trace what happens from the checkout button click through to order confirmation. It responds with the client component that handles the click, the API route it calls, the database write, and the email trigger - each with a file path and line reference. The developer opens two of the cited files to spot-check accuracy, confirms both, and trusts the rest of the trace.
lessons.exercise: Pick a real repository you have access to. In read-only mode, run the guided-tour prompt above in either Claude Code or Cursor, tracing one flow you actually care about. Open at least two of the cited file paths yourself to confirm accuracy.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a structured overview with verifiable file paths, an accurate trace of one real flow, the correct test command, and an honest flag on anything the agent was unsure about rather than a confident guess.
commonMistakes: Trusting the summary without opening any cited files to check it's accurate.
Asking the agent to explain and make edits in the same request, mixing exploration with changes before the mental model is verified.
Skipping the test-command question, then later not knowing how to verify any change the agent makes.
lessons.proTip: If the repo has no CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, or .cursor/rules, this exploration pass is the ideal moment to create one - ask the agent to draft it from what it just found (build/test commands, key conventions, off-limits directories), then edit it yourself before committing. Every future agent session in this repo, in any tool that reads these files, benefits from it.

lessons.title: Write specifications that coding agents implement correctly the first time
lessons.summary: Structure a task spec - goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, definition of done - so Claude Code or Codex implements it correctly with minimal back-and-forth.
lessons.goal: Write a task specification with enough context, constraints, and acceptance criteria that a coding agent implements it correctly on the first pass.
lessons.whyItMatters: The single biggest driver of good or bad agent output is the quality of the instruction it's given. A vague request ('add search to the app') forces the agent to guess scope, data source, and UI - guesses that are expensive to unwind. A tight spec turns a coding agent from a slot machine into a predictable tool, and the same skill transfers directly to writing tickets for human developers.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real, small feature or fix you actually want built - something you could describe to a colleague in under a minute.
steps: State the goal in one sentence: what should exist when this is done, and why.
List acceptance criteria as checkable statements ('user sees an error message if the field is empty'), never adjectives ('better UX').
List constraints and non-goals: what NOT to change, any library/framework restrictions, anything explicitly out of scope.
Name the files or areas likely involved, if you know them - this narrows the agent's search space and reduces wrong guesses.
State how success will be verified: which command to run, which test to pass, what to check manually.
Feed the spec to Claude Code or Codex and ask for a plan before any implementation - Claude Code's Plan Mode (Shift+Tab) does this natively; in Codex, explicitly ask for the plan first.
Check the returned plan against your acceptance criteria before approving implementation.
lessons.prompt:
Task: Add a CSV export button to the Orders table.

Goal: Users can download the currently filtered/visible orders as a CSV file.

Acceptance criteria:
- A button labeled 'Export CSV' appears above the orders table.
- Clicking it downloads a .csv file containing only the rows currently visible (respecting active filters), with the same columns shown in the table.
- If there are zero visible rows, the button is disabled with a tooltip 'No orders to export'.

Constraints:
- Do not change the filtering logic itself.
- Do not add a new backend endpoint - generate the CSV client-side from the data already loaded in the table.
- Do not modify any other page.

Likely files: src/components/OrdersTable.tsx and its existing column config.

Definition of done: the test suite passes, and a manual check confirms the downloaded file's rows match what's on screen.

Before implementing, show me your plan: which files you'll touch and how.
lessons.explanation: Each section closes off one category of ambiguity: the goal prevents scope confusion, acceptance criteria give the agent a checklist instead of vibes, constraints prevent well-intentioned scope creep (like adding a backend endpoint nobody asked for), and the definition of done gives the agent a concrete way to verify its own work instead of declaring victory by assumption. Asking for a plan before code lets you catch a wrong approach while it's still cheap to redirect - this is exactly what Claude Code's Plan Mode is built for, and what a direct 'show me your plan first' instruction does in Codex.
lessons.example: A team lead wants rate limiting added to a login endpoint. A vague version ('add rate limiting to login') risks the agent picking an arbitrary library, threshold, and error format. The spec version states the exact threshold (5 attempts per 15 minutes), the exact response shape (429 with the same JSON error format already used elsewhere in the API), and explicitly excludes touching any other endpoint - producing an implementation that matches what was actually needed on the first pass, with no rework.
lessons.exercise: Pick one real, small feature or fix you want in a project of yours. Write a spec using the template above. Give it to Claude Code or Codex and ask for a plan first; compare the returned plan against your acceptance criteria before letting it implement anything.
lessons.expectedResult: The agent returns a plan that maps clearly onto your acceptance criteria and respects your stated constraints, with little or no need to re-explain the task.
commonMistakes: Writing acceptance criteria as adjectives ('clean', 'better', 'intuitive') instead of checkable statements.
Omitting constraints and non-goals, which lets the agent 'helpfully' touch unrelated code or add infrastructure you didn't want.
Skipping the definition of done, leaving no shared way to know when the task is actually finished.
lessons.proTip: A spec is task-specific; a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md file is standing, repo-wide context (build commands, conventions, off-limits paths) that applies to every future task. Keep them separate - put anything true for every task into the standing context file so you stop repeating it in every spec.

lessons.title: Implement a feature from a written specification with review checkpoints
lessons.summary: Run a full plan, implement, self-test, and diff-review cycle with Claude Code or Codex for a bounded feature, using checkpoints instead of one-shot auto-approval.
lessons.goal: Have a coding agent implement a real, bounded feature end to end, with a plan you approve first and a diff you review before merging.
lessons.whyItMatters: This is the core professional workflow coding agents are built around: not one-shot magic, but a structured loop - plan, implement, verify, review - that keeps a human in control of what actually ships. Doing this well is the difference between 'the agent saved me an afternoon' and 'the agent quietly broke something in production.'
lessons.beforeYouStart: A repository with an existing test suite, and the spec you wrote in the previous lesson (or a similarly structured one). Ideally a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md at the root so the agent already knows build/test commands and conventions.
steps: Paste the spec - goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, definition of done - and explicitly ask for an implementation plan before any code is written.
Review the plan against your acceptance criteria. Reject or redirect anything that touches files outside what you expected.
Once you approve the plan, let the agent implement it in one pass rather than interrupting file by file.
Ask the agent to run the test suite itself and report the result before you look at anything.
Review the diff file by file, not just the summary - look specifically for changes outside the stated scope.
If something looks wrong, describe the specific problem and ask for a targeted fix, not a full re-implementation.
Run the test suite yourself independently before merging, even after the agent reports it passed.
Write or update the CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md if the task revealed a convention worth recording for next time.
lessons.prompt:
Here is the spec for this task:
[PASTE SPEC FROM THE PREVIOUS LESSON]

First, show me your implementation plan: which files you'll create or modify, and the approach for each. Do not write any code yet.

Once I approve the plan, implement it, then run the test suite and report the exact pass/fail result. If any test fails, fix it before reporting completion - do not report done with failing tests.
lessons.explanation: Splitting the request into 'plan first, implementation after approval' creates a cheap checkpoint before any code exists - redirecting a wrong plan costs a sentence; redirecting a wrong implementation costs a rewrite. Requiring the agent to run and report the actual test result, not just claim success, closes the gap between 'looks done' and 'is done.' Reviewing the diff file by file, rather than trusting a prose summary of the change, is what catches scope creep the summary would gloss over.
lessons.example: A developer gives Claude Code the CSV-export spec from the previous lesson. The plan comes back touching OrdersTable.tsx and a new small csvExport.ts utility, matching expectations. After approval, the agent implements it, runs the suite, and reports '42 passed, 0 failed.' The developer reviews the diff and notices the agent also reformatted an unrelated file; they ask for that file to be reverted before merging, keeping the change scoped to exactly what was specified.
lessons.exercise: Take the spec you wrote in the previous lesson (or write a new small one) and run this full plan-approve-implement-verify-review cycle in Claude Code or Codex on a real repo. Do not skip your own independent test run before merging.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a plan you can approve or redirect before any code exists, an implementation that runs its own tests and reports honestly, and a diff scoped to exactly what the spec described - with no surprise edits outside that scope.
commonMistakes: Approving a plan without checking it against every acceptance criterion, then discovering a gap only after implementation.
Trusting a reported 'tests pass' without running the suite yourself before merging.
Reviewing only the agent's prose summary of changes instead of the actual diff, missing out-of-scope edits.
lessons.proTip: For anything beyond a small feature, ask the agent to implement in a separate git worktree or branch rather than your main working directory - Claude Code's worktree support and Codex's sandboxed execution both make this close to zero extra effort, and it means you can keep working elsewhere while the implementation runs.

lessons.title: Debug a failing test with an agentic workflow instead of guessing
lessons.summary: Feed a coding agent the actual failure output and ask it to find and explain the root cause before changing anything, so the fix addresses the real bug instead of just making the test pass.
lessons.goal: Diagnose the true root cause of a failing test with Claude Code or Cursor and apply a fix that's verified against the original failure, not just a green checkmark.
lessons.whyItMatters: Coding agents are very good at making a red test turn green - sometimes by fixing the actual bug, and sometimes by weakening the assertion, adding a special case, or mocking away the failure. Left unchecked, that second pattern quietly erodes test suite value. Directing the agent through root-cause analysis first, and reviewing exactly what changed, turns a fast agent into a trustworthy one.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A repository with a currently failing test (or intentionally break one to practice on) and Claude Code or Cursor set up in it.
steps: Run the failing test yourself first and copy the exact error output - stack trace, assertion message, everything.
Give the agent the failure output and explicitly ask it to explain the root cause before proposing any fix.
Ask it to trace backward from the failure to the specific line(s) of production code responsible, citing file and line.
Review the root-cause explanation critically - does it match what the stack trace actually shows, or is it a plausible-sounding guess?
Only after you accept the root cause, ask for a fix scoped to that cause.
Explicitly forbid changing the test's assertions unless the test itself is proven wrong - state this in the prompt.
Run the full test suite after the fix, not just the one test, to check for regressions elsewhere.
lessons.prompt:
This test is failing. Here is the exact output:
[PASTE FULL ERROR OUTPUT / STACK TRACE]

Do not change any code yet. First:
1. Explain the root cause - trace backward from this failure to the specific production code responsible, citing file and line.
2. State your confidence and what you verified to reach that conclusion.

Do not modify the test's assertions unless you can show the test itself is asserting the wrong thing - if so, explain why explicitly before touching it. Once I confirm your root-cause analysis, propose a fix scoped to that cause only, then run the full test suite (not just this test) and report the result.
lessons.explanation: Separating 'explain the cause' from 'write the fix' into two checkpoints stops the agent from jumping straight to whatever change makes the red test green, which is often the wrong fix. Explicitly forbidding assertion changes without justification closes the most common shortcut - weakening the test instead of fixing the code. Asking for the full suite to run afterward, not just the one test, catches the case where the 'fix' resolves this failure by breaking an assumption something else depended on.
lessons.example: A test asserting that a discount calculation returns $18.00 is failing with $17.995999999999995. A quick agent might 'fix' this by rounding inside the assertion. Asked for root cause first, the agent traces the failure to a floating-point subtraction in the pricing utility and identifies that currency math should use integer cents, not floats - a real bug that would have caused rounding drift in production, not just a flaky test.
lessons.exercise: Find (or intentionally introduce) a failing test in a repo you control. Run the root-cause-first prompt above in Claude Code or Cursor, and don't let it touch the test's assertions until it has shown you a root cause you actually agree with.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a root-cause explanation grounded in the actual stack trace with cited file/line, a fix scoped to that cause rather than the test itself, and a full-suite run confirming no new failures were introduced.
commonMistakes: Accepting 'test now passes' as proof of a correct fix without checking whether the underlying assertion or behavior was weakened.
Letting the agent guess at a root cause from the test name alone instead of the actual error output.
Only re-running the one failing test afterward, missing a regression the fix caused elsewhere.
lessons.proTip: If a bug is hard to reproduce, ask the agent to write a minimal failing test that isolates it before attempting any fix. A precise reproduction is often more valuable than the fix itself, because it stays in the suite and prevents the same bug from coming back.

lessons.title: Refactor an existing module safely without changing its behavior
lessons.summary: Use Claude Code or Cursor to refactor a module in small, test-verified steps, characterizing current behavior first so 'safe' refactor doesn't quietly become a rewrite with new bugs.
lessons.goal: Refactor a real module's internal structure while proving, at each step, that its external behavior hasn't changed.
lessons.whyItMatters: Refactors are the riskiest category of AI-assisted coding because 'looks cleaner' and 'behaves identically' are different claims, and an agent optimizing for the first can silently break the second. A disciplined refactor workflow - characterize behavior, refactor in small steps, verify after each - lets you get the readability and maintainability win without gambling on regressions in code nobody's actively watching.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A module you want refactored that has reasonable test coverage - if it doesn't, budget time to add characterization tests first (see the next lesson on generating tests).
steps: If the module lacks adequate test coverage, stop and add characterization tests first - tests that describe current behavior, not desired behavior.
State the refactor goal precisely: what should improve (e.g. 'split this 400-line function into named steps') and what must NOT change (its public interface, its output for existing inputs).
Ask the agent to propose the refactor as a sequence of small, independently verifiable steps rather than one large rewrite.
Approve and apply one step at a time; run the test suite after each step before moving to the next.
If a step breaks a test, stop there - do not let the agent 'fix' the test to match the new behavior without your explicit review.
Once all steps are applied and tests pass, ask the agent to summarize exactly what changed structurally versus what stayed behaviorally identical.
Do a final manual diff review focused on anything outside the module you named - refactors are where scope creep is most tempting.
lessons.prompt:
I want to refactor [FILE/MODULE PATH]. Goal: [DESCRIBE THE STRUCTURAL IMPROVEMENT, e.g. 'split this into smaller, named functions' or 'extract the validation logic into its own module'].

Hard constraint: the public interface and observable behavior must not change - every existing test must still pass with no modification to test assertions.

Propose this as a sequence of small steps, each independently verifiable by running the test suite. Do not implement all steps at once - show me the sequence first, then implement and I'll approve one step at a time.
lessons.explanation: Breaking the refactor into small, independently verifiable steps means a regression is caught at the step that introduced it, not buried in a 400-line diff at the end. The hard constraint against modifying test assertions is the key guardrail - it forces any behavior change to surface as a visible test failure you have to consciously approve, rather than being silently absorbed by a 'helpful' test update. Asking for a structural-vs-behavioral summary at the end gives you a second, independent check that the refactor did what it claimed.
lessons.example: A 400-line order-processing function needs to be split into named steps for readability. The agent proposes five steps: extract validation, extract pricing, extract tax calculation, extract fulfillment dispatch, then reassemble the orchestrator function. After each step, the full suite runs and passes. On step three, one test fails - the agent flags it rather than adjusting the assertion, and the developer discovers the extraction accidentally dropped a rounding call, catching the bug immediately instead of after the whole refactor was 'done.'
lessons.exercise: Pick a module in one of your own projects that could use structural cleanup and already has test coverage. Run the safe-refactor prompt above in Claude Code or Cursor, approving one step at a time, and stop immediately at any step that breaks a test.
lessons.expectedResult: The refactor completes as a sequence of small, reviewed steps, every existing test still passes with unmodified assertions, and you have a clear structural-vs-behavioral summary of what changed.
commonMistakes: Refactoring a module with no test coverage and treating 'the agent says it's equivalent' as sufficient proof.
Letting the agent apply all proposed steps in one shot instead of verifying after each one.
Allowing test assertions to be adjusted mid-refactor without treating that as a red flag requiring your review.
lessons.proTip: For larger refactors, ask Claude Code to do the work in an isolated git worktree (or use Cursor's background agents) so you can keep the main branch untouched and compare the full before/after diff at the end, rather than reviewing incrementally in your primary working copy.

lessons.title: Generate unit and integration tests that actually catch bugs
lessons.summary: Direct Claude Code or Cursor to write tests that fail without the fix and cover real edge cases, not tautological tests that just mirror the implementation back.
lessons.goal: Generate a test suite for a real function or module that would actually fail if the implementation were broken.
lessons.whyItMatters: AI-generated tests have a well-known failure mode: they restate what the code does rather than what it should do, so they pass even when the code is wrong. A test suite like that gives false confidence - it's worse than no tests in some ways, because it looks like coverage. Directing the agent toward edge cases, boundary conditions, and a red-green check turns test generation from a coverage-percentage exercise into an actual safety net.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A function or module you want tested, ideally one with some real complexity - branching logic, edge cases, or external inputs - not a trivial getter.
steps: Point the agent at the specific function/module and ask it to first list the behaviors and edge cases worth testing, before writing any test code.
Review that list - add anything domain-specific the agent wouldn't know (e.g. a business rule like 'discounts never take a price below zero').
Ask it to write tests covering that reviewed list, including boundary values, empty/null inputs, and at least one deliberately unusual input.
For at least one test, verify the red-green cycle yourself: temporarily break the implementation and confirm the test fails, then restore it and confirm it passes.
Ask the agent to point out any behavior it could not test without more information (e.g. an external API's real error format) rather than faking it silently.
Reject any test that only asserts a function was called, or that mocks so much of the real logic away that nothing meaningful is verified.
lessons.prompt:
Here is the function/module: [PASTE CODE OR FILE PATH]

First, list the distinct behaviors and edge cases worth testing - including boundary values, empty/null/invalid inputs, and any business rules implied by the code. Do not write test code yet.

Once I confirm the list, write tests for each item. Requirements:
- Each test should fail if the underlying logic is wrong, not just if the function isn't called.
- Avoid mocking away the actual logic under test.
- Flag any behavior you can't meaningfully test without more information instead of writing a fake-passing test for it.
lessons.explanation: Asking for the behavior list before any test code separates 'what should be tested' from 'how to test it,' giving you a cheap checkpoint to add domain knowledge the agent can't infer from the code alone. Explicitly banning tests that only check 'was this function called' rules out the most common form of hollow AI-generated test. The manual red-green check on at least one test is the real proof: if you break the code and the test still passes, the whole batch needs re-examination, not just that one test.
lessons.example: A discount-calculation function has an off-by-one edge case at exactly the minimum order threshold. A shallow test suite checks a normal case and a zero-discount case, both of which the buggy code passes. Asked to list edge cases first, the agent identifies 'order value exactly at the threshold' as untested; the resulting test fails against the actual buggy implementation, catching the real bug the shallow version missed.
lessons.exercise: Pick a function in your own codebase with some real branching logic. Run the meaningful-tests prompt above in Claude Code or Cursor. Pick one generated test, deliberately break the implementation, and confirm the test actually fails before restoring the code.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a reviewed list of behaviors and edge cases, a test suite that covers them without hollow assertions, and at least one test you've personally confirmed fails against broken code.
commonMistakes: Accepting high test-count or coverage-percentage as a proxy for quality without checking whether any test would actually fail on a bug.
Letting the agent mock so much of the real logic that the test only verifies its own mocks.
Skipping the manual red-green check and trusting that generated tests are meaningful by default.
lessons.proTip: Ask specifically for at least one integration-style test that exercises the real code path end to end (not just isolated units with everything mocked) - unit tests catch logic errors, but integration tests catch the wiring mistakes between correctly-tested pieces, which is where a surprising number of real production bugs live.

lessons.title: Review a pull request with AI assistance without rubber-stamping it
lessons.summary: Use Codex's automated GitHub review and Claude Code's /code-review as a fast first pass, while keeping the judgment calls on scope, risk, and intent with you, not the agent.
lessons.goal: Use AI code review to catch more issues faster on a real pull request, while still applying your own judgment on the comments before merging.
lessons.whyItMatters: Both Codex and Claude Code can automatically review a pull request and leave comments or a structured findings report, and both are genuinely useful at catching mechanical issues fast. The risk isn't the tool being wrong sometimes - it's a human reviewer treating an AI-approved PR as equivalent to a human-approved one, and rubber-stamping subtle logic or intent problems the agent isn't positioned to catch.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Write access to a repository with Codex's GitHub code review enabled, or Claude Code installed with its /code-review command available, and an open pull request to review (yours or a teammate's, with permission).
steps: Let the automated review run (Codex's GitHub review or Claude Code's /code-review) before you start reading the diff yourself.
Read every comment it leaves, but treat each one as a claim to verify, not a fact - check the cited line in context.
Ask the agent to explain its reasoning on any comment that isn't self-evident, especially anything flagged as a bug or security issue.

Separately, read the diff yourself for the things automated review is weakest at: whether the change actually does what the PR description claims, and whether the change is the right one at all, not just whether the code is well-formed.
Distinguish real findings from noise: dismiss confidently, in writing, any comment that's wrong or out of scope so the next reviewer doesn't re-litigate it.
Only approve once you've personally verified the PR does what it claims to do, on top of whatever the automated review confirmed.
lessons.prompt:
Review this pull request. For each issue you find:
1. State the file and line.
2. Classify it as: bug, security risk, style/convention, or missing test coverage.
3. Explain your reasoning in 1-2 sentences - not just 'this looks wrong,' but why.
4. Rate your confidence (high/medium/low).

Separately, tell me: does this diff actually accomplish what the PR description says it does? If the description and the code seem to disagree, flag that explicitly.
lessons.explanation: Requiring a reasoning sentence and a confidence rating per comment turns a flat list of flags into something you can triage fast - high-confidence security findings get your attention first, low-confidence style nitpicks can be skimmed. The explicit 'does the diff match the description' question targets exactly what automated review tends to miss: intent and scope, as opposed to code mechanics. Asking for this on top of, not instead of, your own read of the diff keeps you accountable for the merge decision.
lessons.example: A PR claims to 'fix pagination off-by-one' but the diff also silently changes the default page size. Automated review flags the off-by-one fix as correct with high confidence, and separately notes (when asked directly) that the default page size change isn't mentioned in the PR description - surfacing a scope mismatch a purely line-by-line review might have missed, which the human reviewer then follows up on with the PR author before approving.
lessons.exercise: Pick an open pull request you have access to (yours or a teammate's, with permission). Run automated review through Codex or Claude Code's /code-review, then use the classify-and-confidence prompt above. Personally verify at least one high-confidence finding by opening the cited file before approving or requesting changes.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a triaged list of findings by type and confidence, an explicit answer on whether the diff matches its stated intent, and you've personally verified at least one finding rather than trusting it blind.
commonMistakes: Treating an AI-approved PR as equivalent to a human-approved one and merging without independent verification.
Reading only the automated comments and skipping your own read of whether the change is the right one, not just well-formed.
Letting low-confidence style nitpicks consume the same attention as high-confidence security findings instead of triaging by severity.
lessons.proTip: Automated review tends to be strongest on mechanical issues (null checks, off-by-ones, missing error handling) and weakest on 'is this the right architectural decision' or 'does this match what we actually discussed in the ticket' - reserve your own attention for exactly the second category, since that's where the agent is least equipped to help.

lessons.title: Plan a migration with AI before touching a single line of code
lessons.summary: Use Claude Code's Plan Mode to produce a phased, risk-assessed migration plan - for a framework upgrade, database change, or API version bump - that you review and revise before any implementation begins.
lessons.goal: Produce a phased migration plan with explicit risk assessment and rollback strategy, fully reviewed, before any code changes start.
lessons.whyItMatters: Migrations - framework upgrades, database schema changes, API version bumps, dependency major-version jumps - are exactly the category of work where a wrong first move compounds. Unlike a single feature, a bad migration step can leave a codebase in a half-migrated state that's harder to finish or revert than to have planned properly. Planning with an agent before touching code lets you pressure-test the approach, surface risks you hadn't considered, and get a phased path with checkpoints, while the cost of changing your mind is still just editing a document.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real migration you're facing or anticipating - e.g. a major framework version bump, moving off a deprecated API, or a database schema change. Claude Code set up in the target repository.
steps: Enter Plan Mode (Shift+Tab in Claude Code) so the session stays read-only while you develop the plan.
Describe the migration goal and constraints: what's changing, what must keep working throughout, and any hard deadline or rollback requirement.
Ask Claude Code to first inventory everything the migration will touch - search the repo for usages, dependencies, and integration points, citing files.
Ask for the migration broken into phases, each independently shippable and revertible, rather than one big-bang change.
For each phase, ask explicitly: what's the risk if this phase goes wrong in production, and what's the rollback path?
Ask what should be verified (tests, manual QA, monitoring) at each phase boundary before proceeding to the next.
Review the plan for gaps yourself - anything the agent couldn't know about (business timing, team capacity, related in-flight work) needs your judgment, not the agent's.
Save the finalized plan as a document (design doc, ticket, or ADR) before starting any implementation session.
lessons.prompt:
I'm planning a migration: [DESCRIBE THE MIGRATION, e.g. 'upgrade from React 17 to React 19' or 'move the users table from a single Postgres instance to a sharded setup'].

Constraints: [WHAT MUST KEEP WORKING THROUGHOUT / DEADLINE / ROLLBACK REQUIREMENTS].

Stay in plan mode - do not edit any files.

First, inventory everything in this repo the migration will touch: search for usages, dependencies, and integration points, citing file paths. Then propose the migration as a sequence of phases, each independently shippable and revertible. For each phase, state: what changes, the risk if it goes wrong in production, the rollback path, and what to verify before moving to the next phase.
lessons.explanation: Staying in Plan Mode for the entire exercise is the key discipline - it removes the temptation to start implementing the moment a plan looks reasonable, keeping the cost of a wrong approach at 'edit a document' rather than 'unwind changed code.' Requiring an inventory pass before the phase plan grounds the plan in what's actually in the repo instead of a generic textbook migration checklist. Asking for risk and rollback per phase, not just for the migration as a whole, is what turns a single big bang into something you can stop safely partway through if something goes wrong.
lessons.example: A team needs to migrate off a deprecated payment SDK before its sunset date. Claude Code's inventory pass finds 14 call sites across 6 files, including one undocumented usage in a background job nobody remembered. The phased plan isolates that background job as its own early phase, precisely because it's the highest-risk, least-visible piece, rather than leaving it bundled into a single large final cutover where a failure would be hardest to isolate.
lessons.exercise: Pick a real migration you're facing or expect to face. Run the migration-planning prompt above in Claude Code, staying in Plan Mode throughout. Review the phased plan for gaps only you would know about, then save the finalized version as a document before starting any implementation.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a phased migration plan grounded in an actual inventory of the repo, with risk and rollback stated per phase, reviewed by you for gaps the agent couldn't know about, saved as a standalone document before any code changes begin.
commonMistakes: Letting the session drift out of plan mode and start implementing before the plan is reviewed and finalized.
Accepting a generic, textbook migration checklist instead of one grounded in an actual inventory of this specific repo.
Treating the agent's plan as complete without adding the business/team context only you have - timing, capacity, related in-flight work.
lessons.proTip: For any migration phase with meaningful production risk, ask explicitly for a feature-flag or dual-write strategy rather than a hard cutover - it's the single highest-leverage question to add to a migration plan, since it turns 'we hope this works' into 'we can verify this safely at low traffic and roll back with a flag flip if it doesn't.'

lessons.title: Set up repository guardrails for safe agent workflows
lessons.summary: Build the standing context files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules) and permission settings that keep Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor working safely and consistently across your team, instead of relying on every developer remembering to type constraints by hand.
lessons.goal: Set up standing context files and permission guardrails so any coding agent working in the repository behaves safely and consistently by default.
lessons.whyItMatters: As more of a team's day-to-day coding runs through agents, the constraints that matter - build/test commands, off-limits directories, coding conventions, what requires human approval - shouldn't live only in each developer's head or in one-off prompts. Encoding them as repo files and permission settings means every agent session, from every developer, in every tool, starts from the same guardrails, and dangerous actions require explicit approval rather than happening by default.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Write access to a real repository your team uses with at least one coding agent. Familiarity with the previous lessons in this path helps but isn't required.
steps: Create CLAUDE.md at the repo root (or run Claude Code's /init) with build/test commands, architecture notes, and conventions - this is read at the start of every Claude Code session.
Create AGENTS.md at the repo root with the same category of information - Codex and Cursor both read this file, so it functions as the cross-tool standard instructions layer.

If the team uses Cursor, add scoped rules under .cursor/rules/*.mdc - short Markdown files with YAML frontmatter (description, alwaysApply, globs) for language- or directory-specific conventions, rather than one giant file.
In every context file, explicitly list off-limits paths or actions - e.g. 'never modify files under /infra without explicit approval,' 'never commit directly to main.'

Set up permission allowlists: in Claude Code, review and commit .claude/settings.json with an appropriate allow/deny list rather than relying on default prompts alone; in Codex, default new sessions to a conservative approval mode (read-only or suggest) rather than full-auto on real repositories.

Add a hook or CI check for anything that must be enforced with code, not prompted for - e.g. a pre-commit or CI step that blocks pushes touching a protected path, regardless of what any agent decided.
Review and update these files periodically - treat them as living documentation that goes stale exactly like any other doc, and correct them when an agent's behavior reveals a gap.
lessons.prompt:
Look at this repository and draft a CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md) covering:
1. Exact build, test, and lint commands.
2. Key architectural conventions (e.g. folder structure, naming, state management approach) - inferred only from what you actually find in the code, not assumed.
3. Directories or files that should never be modified without explicit human approval, and why.
4. Anything a new agent session would otherwise have to rediscover from scratch every time.
Be specific and cite what you found. Flag anything you're inferring versus anything you're unsure about.
lessons.explanation: Asking the agent to draft the context file from what it actually finds in the repo, rather than writing it from a generic template, produces guardrails specific to this codebase's real risks (which directories are actually dangerous, which conventions are actually followed). Requiring it to flag inference versus certainty means you know exactly which lines to double-check before committing the file, since a wrong 'convention' baked into standing context will silently mislead every future session. Explicitly listing off-limits paths turns a vague worry ('I hope it doesn't touch infra') into an instruction every compliant agent reads before it acts.
lessons.example: A team's Cursor sessions kept touching a legacy /billing directory that was mid-deprecation and shouldn't receive new code. Adding one explicit line to AGENTS.md - 'do not add new code to /billing; it is being replaced by /billing-v2, see ADR-014' - stopped the pattern immediately across every developer's sessions, because the constraint now lives in a file every session reads rather than in the memory of whoever happened to mention it that week.
lessons.exercise: In a real repository you maintain, run the context-file draft prompt above with Claude Code or Codex. Review the draft for accuracy, correct anything wrong or assumed, add at least one explicit off-limits rule, and commit the resulting CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md to the repo.
lessons.expectedResult: The repository has a committed, accurate context file that a new agent session reads automatically, including at least one explicit off-limits rule, and you've verified its contents rather than committing an unreviewed draft.
commonMistakes: Writing a generic context file from a template instead of one grounded in what's actually true of this specific repo.

Treating a prompted instruction ('please don't touch /infra') as equivalent to an enforced one (a CI check or permission setting) - prompted instructions can be missed or overridden by a later request in the same session.
Letting the context file go stale after conventions change, so agents keep following guidance that no longer matches the codebase.
lessons.proTip: Split enforcement across the right layer: put things that are genuinely just preferences or context in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/.cursor/rules; put anything that must never happen regardless of what any agent decides, like a push to a protected branch or a change to a secrets file, behind a permission setting or a CI/hook check that runs independent of the agent's judgment.
